claims.text: Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 can initially exist in a high-temperature BCC state.
Phase stability in Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 is governed by a balance between a composition-dependent thermodynamic driving force and diffusion-related kinetic barriers.
A Gibbs-free-energy difference between BCC and competing low-temperature phases provides the thermodynamic driving force for transformation.
An ordered B2 phase is a possible low-temperature competitor to the BCC matrix in this composition.
An incipient FCC phase is a possible low-temperature competitor to the BCC matrix in this composition.
At annealing temperatures with moderately activated diffusion, thermodynamic instability causes gradual formation of an ordered phase from the BCC matrix.
Lower atomic mobility limits the rate and extent of the BCC transformation.
Nucleation and growth of ordered domains within the BCC matrix mediate the change in overall phase stability.
The composition of Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 creates a free-energy difference between its BCC state and a competing ordered phase.
At sufficiently high temperatures, increased atomic mobility overcomes diffusion barriers and permits the thermodynamically driven transformation.
At lower temperatures, kinetic hindrance slows or arrests the transformation by limiting atomic rearrangement.
Controlled lower-temperature annealing will gradually reduce the volume fraction of the metastable BCC phase.
The reduction in BCC phase fraction will be accompanied by nucleation and growth of an ordered phase.
The extent of transformation will correlate with the calculated magnitude of the thermodynamic driving force.
The extent and rate of transformation will vary with annealing temperature and dwell time.
Above the proposed transformation window, the alloy remains single-phase BCC.
Below the proposed transformation window, atomic mobility is too low to produce a measurable transformation.
Microsegregation or unmodeled minor phases may affect the observed phase fractions.

contradictions.description: The mechanism says increasing temperature raises mobility enough to overcome kinetic barriers and enable transformation, whereas the boundary attributes persistence of single-phase BCC at still higher temperature to 'overwhelming kinetic dominance.' High mobility should reduce kinetic arrest; persistence of BCC at high temperature would instead require a thermodynamic-stability explanation or clearer qualification.
